common_name: Obsession Sweet Corn (Vigorous Bicolor Supersweet Hybrid)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees; keep isolated from standard or sugary-enhanced corn to protect kernel sweetness. Obsession is a vigorous supersweet (sh2) bicolor hybrid bred for strong stalk vigor and high-quality ears for Southern home gardens.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Obsession is a supersweet bicolor sweet corn hybrid bred for vigorous stalk growth and consistent ear quality under warm Southern growing conditions. It produces well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels that stay sweet in storage longer than standard sugary-type corn thanks to its supersweet genetics. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, since drought stress at this stage leads to poorly filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.
sources: seed catalog reference (HOSS Tools, University of Florida Seed Program)

common_name: Providence Sweet Corn (Disease-Resistant Bicolor TripleSweet Hybrid)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees; Providence carries resistance to bacterial mottle and downy mildew-related diseases, a useful disease package for a humid main-season Gulf South corn crop.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Providence is a bicolor sweet corn hybrid combining sugary-enhanced tenderness with supersweet-level sugar content, bred with disease resistance including tolerance to bacterial mottle, a bacterial disease that can streak and discolor kernels in warm, wet conditions. It produces large, well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels on sturdy stalks over a main-season 82-day maturity. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill for the best results. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.
sources: seed catalog reference (Stokes Seeds, Rupp Seeds)

common_name: Montauk Sweet Corn (Jumbo-Ear Cool-Soil Bicolor Hybrid)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 60 degrees; Montauk is a synergistic (SE-sh2) bicolor hybrid noted for good vigor in cooler soil than many supersweet types tolerate well, useful for an early Gulf South planting.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Montauk is a synergistic-type bicolor sweet corn hybrid, blending sugary-enhanced and supersweet genetics for excellent flavor and good cool-soil vigor at germination, letting Gulf Coast gardeners plant slightly earlier than standard supersweet types allow. It produces large, jumbo-sized ears packed with tender yellow and white kernels on tall, vigorous stalks. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill for well-filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.
sources: seed catalog reference (Jung Seed, Rupp Seeds, Holmes Seed Company)

common_name: Xtra-Tender 277A Sweet Corn (Warm-Soil Bicolor Supersweet Hybrid)

planting.note: Direct sow only after soil has warmed thoroughly, since supersweet (sh2) types germinate poorly in cool soil; Xtra-Tender 277A is a popular commercial and home-garden bicolor supersweet hybrid widely grown across the South for its tender, high-sugar kernels.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep only once soil has warmed thoroughly, since supersweet corn germinates poorly in cool, wet soil; plant in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination, and keep isolated from standard or sugary-enhanced corn to protect kernel sweetness. Xtra-Tender 277A is a popular bicolor supersweet hybrid known for exceptionally tender, high-sugar kernels that hold their sweetness well after picking, and it is widely grown by both market farmers and home gardeners across warm Southern regions. It produces large, well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels on vigorous stalks. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, and harvest when silks have browned and kernels release a milky juice when pressed.
sources: seed catalog reference (Harris Seeds, 2B Seeds, Demeter Seeds)

common_name: Little Lucy Okra (Dwarf Ornamental-Edible AAS Winner)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; nick or soak seeds overnight to improve germination. Little Lucy is a 1998 All-America Selections-winning dwarf hybrid okra, only about 2 feet tall with burgundy pods and maroon-veined foliage, doubling as an ornamental in a small Gulf Coast bed or container.

directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Little Lucy is a genuine dwarf okra, growing only about 2 feet tall with attractive maroon-veined foliage and burgundy-red pods, making it as much an ornamental accent for a small bed or large container as a food crop. Despite its small stature it produces a real, usable harvest of tender pods best picked young at 2-3 inches, since the compact plant sets pods close together on short internodes. Its diminutive size means it needs no staking and takes up a fraction of the space of full-size okra varieties, a practical advantage for small Gulf Coast gardens where summer heat makes okra one of the most reliable producers. Harvest every couple of days during peak summer heat to keep pods tender and encourage continued flowering.
sources: All-America Selections — Little Lucy okra AAS winner 1998
